title: Designing for Small Hands and Growing Minds: What Research Says About Kids' Interfaces
summary: Children are not small adults. Four bodies of research show how age changes what kids can tap, read, understand and follow on a screen.

body:
Children are not small adults, and the research on how they use screens shows it. Four well-documented findings, from Nielsen Norman Group's usability studies and a randomized trial at the University of Washington, give designers a practical starting point.

## 'Kids' is not one audience

Nielsen Norman Group's Katie Sherwin and Jakob Nielsen (2019) summarize three rounds of usability testing with 125 children aged 3 to 12, run in 2001, 2010 and 2018. Their conclusion is that there is no such thing as designing for children in general. At a minimum, separate ages 3–5, 6–8 and 9–12. The youngest children do not read, early readers read tentatively, and older children scan. NN/g suggests about 14-point text for young children and 12-point for older ones, and avoiding scrolling for the youngest. Children also noticed when content was aimed at a slightly younger or older group and reacted badly; one six-year-old dismissed a site as being for babies. A practical detail from the same research: links meant for parents can sit in a plain text footer, where children rarely click.

## Big targets, simple gestures

In a companion piece, Feifei Liu (2018) reports that motor skills develop unevenly. Children under nine handle tapping and swiping well but struggle with precise dragging, especially with a mouse or trackpad. NN/g recommends touch targets of at least 2 cm × 2 cm for young children, four times the size suggested for adults, and designs that offer two ways to do the same thing, such as tapping a destination or dragging to it. In one test, a five-year-old gave up on a counting game that made a vegetable vanish unless it landed exactly on its circle.

## Symbols that adults see and children miss

Progress bars and cartoon-hand demonstrations seem harmless. But in a randomized controlled trial of 34 preschoolers aged 2 to 5, Alexis Hiniker and colleagues (2016) found that these symbolic elements were entirely inaccessible to children under 3 and needed careful design for ages 3–5. Their review of 94 popular preschool apps found that 44% used at least one of these techniques. Surprisingly, decorating a progress bar with themed imagery made it harder to understand, not easier. The four- and five-year-olds in the study all succeeded with a plain, minimal bar.

## Say what to do, plainly

Liu's second NN/g article (2018) looks at cognition. Children take instructions literally: when a game specifically told a seven-year-old to use the mouse, she abandoned the trackpad she preferred and got frustrated. Better wording is device-neutral, such as click or touch. Games that showed the goal and then how to reach it, with animation and audio, worked well; a game with no instructions left a five-year-old confused. Under-sixes missed subtle character reactions, so feedback should be big and explicit. Familiar metaphors helped too: in a coloring-book app, children reached for an eraser rather than an undo arrow.

## What this means for your design

Pick an age band before you pick a style. Make targets large and forgiving. Prefer plain, direct progress cues to decorated ones. Write instructions that state the goal without naming a device. Keep the limits in mind: NN/g's studies are qualitative with small samples, and the trial included only 11 children between ages 2 and 3, so treat the numbers as starting points and test with real children in your audience.
